title: Delivery
content:
Clusters, pipelines, supply chain, and the AI-assisted layer that is optional by design.
Kubernetes and GitOps Making production match what the repository says, automatically, instead of drifting away from it over a series of careful manual fixes. Search terms: containers, orchestration, Helm, Argo CD, cluster, deployment, GitOps.
Cluster lifecycle: bootstrapping, version skew, control plane upgrades, and node pools that are replaced rather than patched etcd: backup and restore that has actually been tested, defragmentation, and certificate rotation CNI and storage: installing and debugging the network layer, and CSI drivers and their failure modes Workloads: deployments, stateful sets with real volume semantics, daemonsets, and resource requests and limits set from measured usage rather than guesses Packaging: Helm charts built for reuse, Kustomize overlays per environment, and rendering in CI so the applied manifest is reviewable Argo CD: continuous reconciliation, sync windows and waves, self-heal, drift alerting, ApplicationSets across clusters, and project-scoped RBAC so a team cannot sync what it does not own Argo Workflows and Rollouts: DAG-style data and batch pipelines, artifact repositories, and progressive delivery with automated analysis gating canaries on real metrics Operators: writing controllers and CRDs when a Deployment manifest genuinely cannot express the lifecycle Autoscaling: HPA against a useful metric, VPA, KEDA, and cluster autoscaler behaviour under a real workload Networking: Ingress, Gateway API, NetworkPolicy as a default-deny baseline, and service meshes only where the problem is real Podman and rootless containers: where running a daemon as root is not an option, including the UID mapping that quietly breaks volume ownership Troubleshooting under pressure: the ordered path from a failing admission webhook to a pending pod to a CrashLoopBackOff, and what describe does not tell you
CI/CD and Delivery Pipelines The most common engagement we take, and the one where a team’s velocity is either compounding or eroding. Search terms: build automation, automated testing, deployment, release, runner, monorepo.
Platform choice: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, and Drone, chosen to fit the team already rather than to fit our preference Pipeline design: fast feedback on the left, slow and expensive checks on the right, and making the safe path also the quick one so nobody skips it under deadline Reuse: shared workflows, composite actions, pipeline libraries, and conventions that a new service inherits without a meeting Build efficiency: caching layers that do not go stale, matrix builds that fan out where it pays, and cutting a ten-minute pipeline to two Environments and promotion: what moves to staging, what is promoted unchanged, and making the path from merge to production boring Monorepo pipelines: affected-change detection, build graphs, and keeping CI proportional to what actually changed Test strategy: unit, integration, contract, and end-to-end placed by what they catch, with flaky tests treated as bugs rather than retried until green Release engineering: semantic versioning, changelogs generated from commits, image tagging by digest, reproducible builds Secrets in CI: OIDC federation instead of long-lived API keys, scoped permissions, and no credential that outlives the job that needs it Runner strategy: ephemeral and self-hosted runners, isolation between untrusted builds, and keeping build output from being a supply chain attack surface Self-hosted runners on Kubernetes: autoscaled, ephemeral, and not a long-lived machine holding a registration token
Supply Chain Security Making sure nobody can ship compromised code into your production, and that you can prove where any deployment came from. Search terms: SBOM, signing, provenance, dependency, CVE, supply chain, attestation.
SBOM generation: per build, in the format auditors and tooling already consume Signing and verification: Sigstore or cosign, verification at admission, and a cluster that refuses unsigned images Provenance: SLSA-aligned build attestations, so an artefact can be traced to the source and the workflow that produced it Dependency management: pinning, update automation with review rather than blind merging, and lockfiles treated as security controls Vulnerability management: scanning that produces triage rather than a dashboard nobody reads, with severity weighed against exploitability in the actual environment Hardening the pipeline itself: least-privilege workflow permissions, pinned third-party actions by digest, and pullrequest versus pullrequest_target handled correctly
AI-Assisted Delivery This is a genuinely optional layer, and a client gets the same pipeline whether they take it or not. The useful question is never "do you use AI" but "does it measurably beat what you have now, and what happens when it is wrong".
Where it earns its place Test generation: coverage on the paths that need it, reviewed as carefully as the code it covers Review assistance: first-pass review for correctness, security smells, and missed cases, with a human owning the merge decision Pipeline debugging: reading a failed job, correlating the logs, and proposing the fix rather than leaving a wall of output Migration and bulk change: the mechanical parts of a framework or language upgrade, where volume is the problem and review is the bottleneck Documentation from the code: keeping runbooks and reference docs from drifting out of date Flaky test triage: identifying the ordering or timing assumption behind an intermittent failure
What we do not do with it No unreviewed code to production. Every change is read by a person who is accountable for it No secrets or production data into a model. Bounded context, and the pipeline is designed so a leak is not possible No self-hosted models on client infrastructure unless asked. The default is a vendor under an agreement the client has reviewed No capability claimed without a baseline. If it does not measurably beat the manual path on your workload, it does not go in No added dependency on a provider’s model. Swapping it out stays possible, and the fallback is designed in from the start
